rows.evidence: Q1: sections 'ET-based irrigation scheduling and irrigation technology' and 'Corn to cotton conversion' - authors compute their own irrigation demand estimates (Eqs 1-8, Table VI, Figs 7-8) from Agri-Partners applied-depth data and TWDB data.
rows.notes: The study's own result on subsurface drip irrigation does not show water conservation: Table VI gives SDI cotton applied depth 274 mm and FIR 1.01, essentially identical to centre pivot (274 mm, FIR 1.03), and the authors state in the corn-to-cotton section that choosing SDI over spray or LEPA may not necessarily result in less irrigation demand. SDI area was assumed negligible in the demand-reduction scenarios. Higher SDI cotton yield (1.48 vs 1.17 Mg/ha) implies better water use efficiency, but statements that SDI improves yield/WUE/soil temperature are citations of other work (Bordovsky and Porter 2003; Colaizzi et al. 2004-2006), not this study's result. Hence no own evidence that drip delivers water conservation.

rows.evidence: Q1: sections on ET-based scheduling and corn-to-cotton conversion - own computations of FIR and demand volumes (Eqs 1-8, Table VI, Fig 7). Q2: Table VI and following text - fields managed with the TXHPET network under Agri-Partners had FIR generally below the TWDB (mixed) values (e.g. corn CP 0.86 vs 1.18; cotton CP 1.03 vs 1.28) with yields seldom reduced, which the authors conclude shows withdrawals could be reduced by greater network adoption; doubling network-managed area estimated to cut demand 14% (Fig 7). Q4: Eqs 3-5 and Table VI - the study computes the seasonal net irrigation requirement from ETc and precipitation and the fraction of requirement applied (FIR), i.e. the over-application that ET scheduling removes. Q5: Table VI reports FIR/applied depths separately for six crops (corn, cotton, sorghum, peanut, soybean, wheat) and Fig 7 gives demand separately for Northern and Southern High Plains. Q6: Agri-Partners data cover about 20 000 ha on 450 commercial fields across the Northern High Plains, with county- and season-weighted FIR compared against regional TWDB volumes for the 39-county area. Q8: text after Table VI - authors note Agri-Partner yields may reflect higher management level, USDA data likely include pest/weather-damaged and grazed fields, and TWDB demand by irrigation technology was unavailable; also average depths may include conveyance losses.
rows.notes: The 14% and 21% savings are scenario projections from a demand model not validated against observed regional pumping; the supporting evidence is the observational FIR comparison. Q3 no: single method (applied-depth comparison feeding one model). Q7 no: conditions mentioned (peanut pegging-stage moisture, adoption fraction t) are explanations or scenario variables, not stated requirements. Q9 no: no SD, CI or uncertainty propagation; the 14-21% spread is a scenario range.

notes: Paper is part historical review (irrigated area, technology trends from TWDB surveys) and part original analysis (own irrigation-demand calculations from Agri-Partners and TWDB data). Rated as primary on the basis of the original demand analysis; the review portions and cited results from other studies were not counted. Full text appears complete.
